clinicalPearls: A rare disorder combining continuous muscle stiffness (myotonia-like activity) with a skeletal chondrodysplasia, usually presenting in infancy or early childhood
Characteristic facial appearance includes blepharophimosis with narrowed palpebral fissures, puckered lips, a fixed pursed expression and low-set ears
Generalised muscle stiffness produces a stiff gait, muscle hypertrophy and difficulty opening the eyes and mouth
Skeletal features include short stature, joint contractures, kyphoscoliosis and bony dysplasia on imaging
Caused by mutations in HSPG2 encoding perlecan, a heparan sulphate proteoglycan of the basement membrane and cartilage, inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern
The sustained muscle activity is largely of peripheral nerve and muscle origin and, unlike a pure channelopathy, can show complex continuous discharges on electromyography
Antimyotonic agents such as sodium-channel-blocking drugs and other muscle-relaxant strategies can reduce the stiffness
reference.pathophysiology: Schwartz-Jampel syndrome is caused by mutations in HSPG2, which encodes perlecan, a large heparan sulphate proteoglycan that is a major structural and signalling component of basement membranes and of cartilage extracellular matrix. Deficient or dysfunctional perlecan disrupts cartilage development, producing the chondrodysplasia, short stature and skeletal deformities. At the neuromuscular junction, perlecan anchors acetylcholinesterase in the synaptic basal lamina, and its deficiency reduces cholinesterase activity so that acetylcholine action is prolonged, contributing, together with abnormal muscle-membrane excitability, to the sustained muscle activity and stiffness that clinically resembles myotonia.
additionalDifferentials: Isaacs syndrome (neuromyotonia) and other peripheral nerve hyperexcitability syndromes
Congenital myasthenic syndromes with abnormal cholinesterase
Skeletal dysplasias with contractures and stiff joints
additionalInvestigations: Electromyography showing continuous complex repetitive and myotonic-like discharges
Serum creatine kinase, which may be normal or mildly elevated
Skeletal survey and imaging to characterise the chondrodysplasia and contractures
Ophthalmological and orthopaedic assessment for eye and skeletal complications
Muscle biopsy where the diagnosis remains uncertain
redFlags: Feeding or airway difficulty in infancy from facial and jaw stiffness
Susceptibility to anaesthetic complications, including reported concern about malignant-hyperthermia-like reactions and difficult airway
Severe joint contractures limiting mobility and function
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies with severity, but many children with the classic form survive into adulthood with persistent stiffness and skeletal deformity, whereas a rarer severe neonatal presentation carries higher early morbidity; the disorder is generally non-progressive once established but causes lasting orthopaedic and functional handicap.
pitfalls: Attributing the stiffness to a pure muscle channelopathy and missing the skeletal chondrodysplasia that defines the syndrome
Overlooking the anaesthetic and airway risks in a child with facial and jaw stiffness
Confusing the continuous discharges with the discharges of Isaacs syndrome or true myotonia
Failing to arrange orthopaedic and ophthalmological surveillance for the skeletal and eye complications
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Reduce the myotonia-like muscle stiffness with membrane-stabilising agents such as carbamazepine, phenytoin or the antiarrhythmic mexiletine
Provide physiotherapy, stretching and orthopaedic management for joint contractures, kyphoscoliosis and skeletal deformity
Offer ophthalmological treatment for blepharophimosis and related eye complications, including surgical correction where vision or lid closure is affected
Address feeding and airway difficulty from facial and muscle involvement, and flag the anaesthetic risk of a difficult airway and perioperative complications before surgery
Support growth, mobility and function with occupational therapy and mobility aids
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across neurology, orthopaedics, ophthalmology and rehabilitation
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive HSPG2 (perlecan) disorder and screen at-risk relatives
